title: The Laws of War
summary: Moses gives Israel rules for warfare. Before battle a priest reminds the army that the LORD fights for them, and officers send home the man with a new house, an unharvested vineyard, a fiancée, or a fearful heart. Distant cities are offered peace before any siege, while the cities of Canaan are to be devoted to destruction, and fruit trees are to be spared during a siege.
story: Israel is about to cross the Jordan into a land held by walled cities and armed peoples, so it is no surprise that the law code turns to war. Chapter 20 belongs with the laws of chapters 19 to 25 that govern life, death, and justice in the land. It looks back to the defeat of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan (chapters 2 and 3) and forward to the wars of Joshua and Judges. Its first word is fear, and its answer is the memory of the exodus: the God who brought Israel out of Egypt goes with them now. The chapter also shows the limits God places on war, and in verses 16-18 it states the command about the Canaanite cities that makes the conquest so troubling to modern readers.
historical:
War in the ancient Near East was brutal. Assyrian royal inscriptions from the ninth to seventh centuries BC boast of cities burned, captives impaled, and orchards cut down, and Assyrian palace reliefs show soldiers felling trees around a besieged city. Cutting down an enemy's fruit trees was a way to ruin a region for years. Against that background, verses 19-20 stand out: Israel may use non-fruit trees for siege works, but it must not destroy the trees that feed people.

The Old Testament's own history shows these laws in use. Gideon sends home everyone who is afraid before his battle with the Midianites (Judges 7:3), echoing verse 8. Centuries later, 1 Maccabees 3:56 records Judas Maccabeus dismissing men who were building houses, newly betrothed, planting vineyards, or fainthearted, according to the law, before fighting the Seleucid army in the second century BC. The command to devote the Canaanite cities to destruction was applied at Jericho and Ai (Joshua 6 and 8), though the biblical narratives also record many Canaanites living on in the land (Judges 1).
cultural:
Israel had no standing army at this point. Its soldiers were farmers and tradesmen called up from their villages, which is why the exemptions in verses 5-7 matter. A man who had built a house but not dedicated it, planted a vineyard but not eaten from it (a new vineyard took several years to produce), or become engaged but not married was allowed to go home. These were the goods of ordinary life that the land promised, and the law would not let war rob a man of them before he had tasted them. The exemption for the fearful was practical as well as merciful: fear spreads through an army.

The word translated devote to complete destruction refers to the practice called herem (the ban). Something under the ban was set apart entirely to God and removed from human use, whether by destruction or by being given to the sanctuary. The same concept appears in the Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription from the ninth century BC, in which King Mesha says he devoted the people of the Israelite town of Nebo to destruction for his god. The idea was known across the region; what the Bible does with it is the subject of the hard question below.
literary: The chapter is built as a series of speeches and laws. The priest's address (verses 2-4) begins with Hear, O Israel, the opening words of the Shema in 6:4, which makes the battle speech an act of worship. The officers' four questions (verses 5-8) follow a repeated pattern of question, command, and reason: Let him return home, or he may die in battle. The central laws distinguish between distant cities (verses 10-15) and the cities of the land (verses 16-18). The chapter ends with a law about trees phrased as a question, which gives the passage an unexpectedly gentle close.

outline.t: Do not fear: the LORD fights for you
Terms for distant cities: peace offered first
The cities of Canaan devoted to destruction

doctrines.note: Israel is not to measure its chances by counting horses and chariots. Courage rests on remembering what God has already done in the exodus and trusting his presence in the present battle.

The command to devote the Canaanite cities to destruction is presented as God's judgment on the detestable practices of the land (verse 18; compare Genesis 15:16), and as protection against Israel adopting them. It is limited to a particular people and time, not a general rule of war.
Even in war the created world is not simply a resource to be wasted. The trees that feed people are to be spared, a reminder that the land and its fruit belong to God.

words.note: Charam, to devote to destruction or put under the ban. It means to set something apart irrevocably for God, removing it from ordinary use. The noun herem comes from the same root. In war texts it means total destruction, but the word also appears in non-military settings for things permanently dedicated to God.

Shalom, peace. The word ranges from the absence of war to wholeness and well-being. In verse 10 it means a treaty of peace offered to a city before any siege. Israel's wars were supposed to begin with an offer to end them.

Yare, to fear. The chapter opens with do not be afraid and later sends the fearful home. Deuteronomy uses the same verb for the reverent fear of God; the point is that the right fear drives out the wrong one.

Ets, tree. The chapter ends with trees, not soldiers. Verse 19 asks whether the trees of the field are human, that they should be besieged, a question that turns an act of war into an act of restraint.

christ: The priest's words, that the LORD goes with you to fight for you, sound a theme that runs through the whole Bible: salvation is God's battle, won by him on behalf of his people. The New Testament carries that theme forward but changes its weapons. Jesus tells Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52), and Paul says that the church's struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual powers, fought with truth, righteousness, and the gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:12-17). The New Testament presents the cross as God's decisive victory over those powers (Colossians 2:15). The holy war of Deuteronomy is therefore not a model for Christian violence; the link to Christ is the pattern of a God who fights for his people, and who in Christ wins by suffering rather than by the sword.

hard.q: How can God command the destruction of the Canaanite cities, sparing nothing that breathes?
hard.a:
This is one of the hardest passages in the Old Testament, and Christians and Jews have wrestled with it for centuries. Several responses are offered, often in combination. The first reads the command as God's judgment on nations whose practices, including child sacrifice (18:10), had filled up their guilt over centuries, as Genesis 15:16 anticipates, and it notes that the same God later judged Israel by exile for the same sins. The second notes that the language of total destruction was a standard feature of ancient war reports, which often used sweeping, hyperbolic terms, and points out that the books of Joshua and Judges themselves describe Canaanites still living in the land after the conquest. On this reading the command may have aimed at driving out and dismantling Canaanite religion and power rather than literal extermination. A third view, held by some Christian interpreters, sees these texts as a real but partial stage in God's self-revelation, to be read in the light of Christ.

The Bible itself limits the command: it applies only to the named peoples of Canaan, not to Israel's other wars (verses 10-15), and it is never given as a pattern for later generations. The texts also record exceptions such as Rahab and the Gibeonites (Joshua 2 and 9). Readers should feel the weight of the passage rather than rush past it, while recognizing that it gives no permission for violence in God's name today; where Christians have used these texts that way (as in some crusading and colonial rhetoric), the church has come to see it as a misuse.

questions: Israel's courage was to come from remembering the exodus. What past acts of God do you return to when you are afraid?
The law sent home the man with a new house, a new vineyard, or a bride to be. What does that suggest about how God values ordinary life?
The chapter ends by protecting fruit trees in the middle of a war. What would restraint look like in the conflicts you are part of?
